content: Participants in the high-intensity exercise group demonstrated greater improvements in VO2max compared to those in the moderate-intensity exercise group. However, no significant differences in VO2max were observed between participants in the combined aerobic exercise and diet/nutrition counseling group and those in the diet/nutrition counseling group alone. All point estimates for VO2max improvements exceeded 2 mL/kg/min, indicating a potentially clinically meaningful enhancement in cardiorespiratory fitness among exercisers, with greater improvements noted in high-intensity exercise compared to moderate-intensity exercise. The duration of exercise interventions ranged from 12 to 16 weeks, with participants exercising three times per week for 45 to 135 minutes per session. Maximum heart rate (HRmax) was assessed, and participants in the aerobic exercise intervention group exhibited a reduction of 91 beats per minute compared to the non-exercising control group. No significant differences in HRmax were observed between the combined aerobic and progressive resistance exercise (PRE) group and the non-exercising control group. Heterogeneity was present in the meta-analyses, likely due to variations in exercise interventions across studies. Exercise duration ranged from 20 to 120 minutes per session, three times per week, over 12 to 52 weeks. However, point estimates for exercise time did not reach the 5-minute threshold for clinical importance. Strength outcomes were assessed in several studies, with significant improvements in upper and lower body strength observed in the combined aerobic and PRE group compared to the non-exercising control group. Meta-analyses revealed clinically meaningful increases in strength, with point estimates exceeding 2 kg for upper extremities and 5 kg for lower extremities. Participants in the PRE group demonstrated greater strength gains compared to those in the aerobic exercise-only group. The age of participants in the studies ranged from 18 to 66 years, with approximately 70% being male. Exercise interventions included aerobic, resistance, and combined training, with durations ranging from 6 to 52 weeks. Significant improvements in VO2max were observed in response to aerobic and concurrent training, but not resistance training alone. Improvements in sub-maximal heart rate and exercise time were also noted among exercisers compared to non-exercisers, although these findings were not always statistically significant. Meta-analyses of strength outcomes showed significant increases in upper and lower body strength, as measured by one-repetition maximum (1-RM) for chest press and knee flexion. Non-significant trends toward improvement were observed for leg press and knee extension. Combined exercise and testosterone interventions showed a non-significant trend toward increased strength compared to testosterone alone. Heterogeneity was present in several meta-analyses, attributed to differences in exercise interventions, outcomes assessed, and participant characteristics. Multimodal exercise interventions, including aerobic, resistance, and flexibility training, demonstrated significant improvements in cardiovascular fitness, strength, and flexibility. Studies using progressive resistance training (PRT) interventions reported significant strength gains in the intervention group compared to controls. Tai chi interventions showed significant improvements in flexibility and cardiovascular outcomes, while yoga interventions did not result in changes in functional capacity. Overall, exercise interventions were associated with significant improvements in strength, cardiovascular fitness, and flexibility compared to non-exercising controls. However, heterogeneity across studies and variations in intervention types and outcomes limited the ability to perform meta-analyses in some cases. Despite these limitations, the findings support the clinical importance of exercise in improving physical fitness and health outcomes.
